item.research_question: How does substrate deposition temperature influence the phase evolution, microstructure, and mechanical properties of HfNbTiVZr high-entropy thin films compared to bulk alloys?
item.material_system: HfNbTiVZr near-equimolar thin films (XPS determined composition: Hf21Nb20Ti20V18Zr21)
item.processing_route: Non-reactive DC-magnetron sputtering in ultra-high vacuum (<5 × 10−8 Pa) using elemental targets; substrates (Si(001) or Al2O3(00l)) biased to −50 V and heated to three temperatures: room temperature (RT), 275 °C, and 450 °C.
item.test_conditions: Mechanical properties measured via nanoindentation (Berkovich tip); structural analysis via XRD, pole figures, and TEM/SAED; chemical analysis via XPS and EDS.
key_findings: Films deposited at room temperature exhibit an amorphous microstructure with a hardness of 6.5 ± 0.3 GPa.
Films deposited at 275 °C crystallize into a single-phase body-centred cubic (bcc) solid solution with a hardness of 7.9 ± 0.3 GPa.
Films deposited at 450 °C on Si substrates form a dual-phase structure of bcc matrix and C15 Laves phase precipitates, reaching a peak hardness of 9.2 ± 0.4 GPa.
Films deposited at 450 °C on sapphire substrates form a dual-phase structure of bcc matrix and C14 Laves phase precipitates.
The lattice parameter of the bcc phase decreases from 3.42 Å (at 275 °C) to 3.39 Å (at 450 °C).
All thin films exhibit significantly higher hardness than reported literature values for bulk HfNbTiVZr alloys (3.8 GPa).
Films deposited at 275 °C show a strong <110> preferred orientation, while films at 450 °C on Si show a shift to <100> orientation.
item.mechanism: The high quenching rates (>10^6 K/s) during magnetron sputtering combined with low ad-atom mobility at low temperatures enable the synthesis of amorphous phases not accessible in bulk. At higher temperatures, surface diffusion is much faster than bulk diffusion, allowing segregation and Laves phase formation at lower temperatures (450 °C) than in bulk annealing (>600 °C). The specific Laves phase (C14 vs C15) depends on the substrate, likely due to differences in diffusivities and Nb availability during growth.
item.limitations: Peak overlaps in the θ–2θ diffractograms for films on sapphire at 450 °C did not allow unambiguous separation between the hcp phase and the C14 Laves phase, though the latter was favored based on lattice parameter stability and pole figure fits.
item.future_work: Further studies are required to determine why the substrate affects the C14/C15 formation and to understand the role of Nb diffusivity and availability during film growth compared to solid-state transformation.
quotes: Films deposited at room temperature exhibit an amorphous microstructure and are 6.5 GPa hard.

A higher deposition temperature (450 °C) leads to the formation of C14 or C15 Laves phase precipitates in the bcc matrix and a further enhancement of mechanical properties with a peak hardness value of 9.2 GPa.

The formation of Laves phases in the thin films, at much lower temperatures than during annealing of bulk samples, can be explained by the fact that surface diffusion (relevant during growth of the film) is typically much faster than bulk diffusion.
